tier_reason: The paper (accepted at ALENEX26) benchmarks PHast/PHast+ against PTHash in Tables 5.2/5.3. It states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5600G), the compilers (rust 1.84.1, gcc 12.2.0) and the flags (third-level plus CPU-native optimizations). The benchmark code is public: ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments src/tablePHast.cpp with rust/src/phast_contender.rs, and the exact paper fork is on figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.30272380.v6, GPL-3.0+).

corrections.workload: MPHF-Experiments framework: MPHF construction (1 and 12 threads) and queries on 5*10^7 and 5*10^8 random string keys, each of uniformly random length 10-50 bytes (Tables 5.2/5.3 of arXiv:2504.17918). Uniformly random 64-bit integer keys were used only for parameter tuning (Sec. 5.1) and the ablation study (Sec. 5.4). Measures bits/key, query ns/query, and construction ns/key.
corrections.caveats: First-party paper by the PHast authors (Beling, Sanders); the ph crate author is the first author. At 5*10^7 keys, single-thread PHast construction (606 ns/key for S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) is slightly slower than PTHash (577 ns/key). PHast wins on query time (10 vs 54 ns), space (1.94 vs 2.11 bits/key), and 12-thread construction (69 vs 231 ns/key). PtrHash is close on queries, and at 5*10^8 keys it catches up with and may overtake PHast+ (3.2). The comparison is only against other MPHFs (PTHash, PTHash-HEM, PHOBIC, PtrHash, SIMDRecSplit, SicHash, FMPH, FMPHGO, FiPS, Bipartite ShockHash). It does not compare against std::unordered_map or CMPH. The paper left BBHash out of its tests because FMPH is its improved counterpart. GitHub's license detector reports only Apache-2.0, but the README and ph/Cargo.toml state the dual license 'MIT OR Apache-2.0'.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match Table 5.2 exactly (PHast S=8 lambda=4.3 EF 1.94/10/606/69; PTHash lambda=5.0 EF 2.11/54/577/231; PHast+ 61-140 ns/key single-thread construction and 10-15 ns queries). One fix: the comparison tables use random 10-50-byte strings, not 64-bit integers. Metadata verified: 173 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-25.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (the arXiv comment says 'ESA version') compares MorphisHash with ShockHash in Sec. 6.1/Fig. 2 and Table 1 on 100M keys. It uses the public MPHF-Experiments code (src/tableMorphisHash.cpp) and states the CPU (Intel Core i7-11700). It does not state the compiler or flags, so it cannot be tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: MorphisHash saves Theta(ln n) bits in expectation vs ShockHash, 'a factor of 20 less space overhead in practice'. That factor is for a single unpartitioned base case (Sec. 6.1, Bipartite MorphisHash with b=n-6): under 0.1 bits of total overhead vs about 2 bits for Bipartite ShockHash, at the cost of about 4x more seed tests. For a full MPHF on 100M keys (Table 1), Bip. MorphisHash-RS (n=52, b=n-4) gives 1.501 bits/key, 137 ns/query and 6,669 ns/key construction. Bip. ShockHash-RS (n=66) gives 1.523 bits/key, 147 ns/query and 7,186 ns/key. This is about 0.02 bits/key, or 27% less overhead, at equal construction time. At an equal 1.489 bits/key, MorphisHash-RS builds in 8,085 ns/key vs 172,738 ns/key for ShockHash-RS, which the paper calls about 21x faster construction.
corrections.workload: (1) A single Bipartite MorphisHash vs Bipartite ShockHash base case (n up to about 64 keys): idealized space overhead and average successful seed (Figs. 2-3). (2) Partitioned MorphisHash-RS/-Flat vs Bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat (and CONSENSUS-RS, PHOBIC) on 100 million keys in the MPHF-Experiments framework: space (bits/key), query time (ns/query) and construction time (ns/key) (Table 1, Fig. 5).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core, 16 MiB L3), 64 GiB dual-channel DDR4-3200
corrections.caveats: The '20x less space overhead' figure applies to the per-base-case redundancy of ShockHash, not to total bits/key. For full 100M-key MPHFs, the gain is about 0.01-0.02 bits/key at equal construction time, or about 21x faster construction at equal space (1.489 bits/key). The paper does not state the compiler or flags; the MorphisHash and MPHF-Experiments CMake files default to a Release build with -march=native. The baseline (ShockHash) is an advanced research MPHF by the same group, not std::unordered_map, CMPH or BBHash. Single-author paper that uses the group's own benchmark framework. The repo is a GitHub fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash with 3 stars. The newest commit on any branch is 2025-07-03 (the pushed_at of 2025-11-13 adds no newer commit).

notes: The full paper text was readable from the arXiv PDF (v2). The abstract numbers are verbatim, and I added Table 1 figures to give the '20x' claim its real context. I corrected last_commit (2025-07-03 on main; the dev and compCount branches are older), which makes the repo stale.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The full PHOBIC paper (ESA 2024) compares PHOBIC-GPU against CPU PHOBIC in Table 1 and Fig. 6a. It states the CPU (Intel Core i7-11700), the GPU (Nvidia RTX 3090, Vulkan 1.3.236), the compiler (GCC 11.4.0) and the flags (-march=native -O3). The benchmark code is public: ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments src/tablePhobic.cpp (a 'CPU vs GPU' block plus GpuPhobicContender and PhobicContender rows), and stefanfred/PHOBIC-GPU benchmark.cpp.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PHOBIC-GPU constructs an MPHF at 2.17 bits/key in 28 ns/key (GPU + 8 CPU threads), and the MPHF answers queries in 37 ns on the CPU (abstract, Table 1). At lambda=9.0 with interleaved Rice coding, PHOBIC-GPU gives 1.76 bits/key, 52 ns/query and 27 ns/key construction. CPU PHOBIC gives 1.74 bits/key, 50 ns/query, 9,171 ns/key (1 thread) and 1,781 ns/key (8 threads). The paper states a 62x construction speedup over the multithreaded CPU implementation and about 30x lower energy (Table 1, Sec. 5.2 of arXiv:2404.18497).
corrections.workload: MPHF construction on 100 million random string keys (random length 10-50 characters). GPU construction (plus 8 CPU threads) is compared with CPU PHOBIC at 1 and 8 threads, for the same configurations (lambda=9, 13, 14; interleaved Rice/Compact coding). All queries run on the CPU.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core), 64 GiB DDR4, Ubuntu 22.04.1; GPU: Nvidia RTX 3090
corrections.caveats: The speedup compares an RTX 3090 GPU with an 8-thread i7-11700 CPU, so it depends on the hardware. The paper notes the GPU only wins for large n and large lambda; at small lambda, transferring the input to the GPU dominates. Queries are not faster: they run on the CPU and are the same as CPU PHOBIC. The system draws about 405 W during the GPU search vs 195 W for the multithreaded CPU. Needs a Vulkan-capable GPU. The baseline is the authors' own CPU PHOBIC (jermp/pthash phobic branch), not std::unordered_map, CMPH or BBHash. Only 4 GitHub stars, and the last commit was 2025-07-03.

notes: The full PDF was readable. The abstract numbers are verbatim and Table 1 supports the CPU-vs-GPU speedup. The ratio derived from Table 1 (1,781/27, about 66x) differs slightly from the 62x stated in the text, so the claim cites the paper's own 62x. I upgraded the tier to A because the paper states the compiler, flags, CPU and GPU, and the benchmark code is public.
